provisions.finding: Plant means living plants/parts. Plant product means processed or natural plant-based product exposed to pest-introduction/distribution risk because of its nature or processing. The risk phrase qualifies the class; processed origin alone is insufficient.

Other regulated articles are pest-capable objects deemed to require quarantine measures. Wood packaging excludes paper products. Commodity and consignment definitions remain limited to plants, plant products and other regulated articles.

Post-harvest pests and prevention during processing/storage are recognized. These general surveillance/control provisions do not independently require an import permit for every clean manufactured food. They preserve action against actual postprocessing contamination.

Scientific/PRA basis, import permits and release authorization attach to the defined plant/plant-product/regulated-article classes. Article4(4) addresses the restricted list, rather than bringing all nonregulated manufactured products within the law. The awkward English4(2) calls its origin-related document an import permit; no silent relabelling as a phytosanitary certificate is needed for the excluded-class inference.

Wood packaging has independent treatment/logo conditions. The scenario should use clean factory retail packing and paper/cardboard/plastic outer packaging without wood, soil, straw or raw plant filler.

The authority must discharge IPPC obligations under national law; delegated measures must accord with this Proclamation and relevant international phytosanitary standards. This is operative standards context, not mere international membership, but neither clause creates automatic direct adoption of every illustrative ISPM category.

Inspectors may inspect defined goods, suspend suspect consignments, collect samples and act on regulated pests. Ordinary truthful customs declaration and arrival inspection remain. No independent all-food import duty appears here.

foodArrivalPeerReview.scope: Paid 100 g factory-sealed Japanese plain industrially steamed, rolled and dried Camellia tea for personal drinking. No separately obtained permits, certificates, agency registration or advance notice; ordinary customs and arrival inspection/fees allowed.
foodArrivalPeerReview.conclusion: A defensible lawful route exists through destination inspection under regulation7, applied for by ordinary accurate customs declaration under regulation8(1) upon arrival. No independent preobtained CoC, exemption letter or digital conformity mark is established for tea on that route. Mandatory standards compliance, possible testing/fees and the authority-issued import clearance certificate remain. This is a combined-provision legal interpretation, not an assurance of immediate or cost-free postal release.

routeAnalysis.finding: Schedule 1 Part 1 Group X includes food and food products. Regulation 6 expressly applies assessment whether goods are for trade or personal use. No invented personal-food exemption is needed.

Regulations 5(2), 5(5)(a) and Schedule 1 Part 2 item 1 exempt consignments with FOB value at most USD 2,000 (except used vehicles) from pre-export verification. Regulation 8(2)(i) can require an exemption letter where applicable to a regulation 5(5) route. However, regulation 7(1) expressly operates notwithstanding regulation 5 and directs destination inspection for Part 1 goods lacking a CoC. It does not restrict that alternative to higher-value goods or exclude goods also satisfying Part 2. Food remains Group X even when low-value. Regulation 10(1)(a) repeats the no-CoC destination route. Entry need not rest on a letter-dependent exemption.

routeAnalysis.issue: Does automatic low-value status compel a letter regardless of route?
routeAnalysis.finding: Strongest contrary reading: regulation 5(5)(a) says the goods shall be exempt, and 8(2)(i) points to 5(5), so low-value goods might routinely be channelled into exemption-letter verification. Preferred reading: the automatic exemption removes origin verification; it neither prohibits destination inspection nor imposes an unconditional letter duty. Regulation 7 expressly overrides regulation 5, while 8 requires a letter only where applicable. A universal letter prerequisite would obstruct regulation 7 despite its unqualified no-CoC trigger. This does not mean every low-value exemption procedure is letter-free, or guarantee whether a surcharge will be imposed.

Regulation 8(1) defines the application as an accurate customs declaration through the electronic single window, before or upon arrival. Regulation 8(2)(a–e) lists normal transport, packing, invoice, customs and transit records; the foreign CoC in (f) and exemption letter in (i) are conditional. Japanese plain tea does not fall within the EAC product-permit, vehicle export-certificate, returning-resident passport or diplomatic-note categories. Regulations 7(3) and 10(6) direct the inspector to issue the ICC after conformity is established; regulation 12 requires it before release. This ICC is the output of arrival inspection, not a special document the Japan store must obtain beforehand.

SI 112/2022 regulation 13(3) requires pre-clearance evidence of digital marks only for Certification Regulations 2021 Schedule 3 Part II categories. The complete schedule lists cosmetics, electricals and construction materials, not tea or food. Full SI 108/2022 section 13 only changes the fee from 18 to 21 shillings per unit. Section 2 retains the Part II cross-reference; section 11 inserts regulation 23A(1), a conformity duty, and 23A(2), a marking duty for locally manufactured Part II goods. The amendment does not extend digital marks to tea. Manufacturing certification under 2021 regulation 4 is not a general private-import permit.

The official 8 September 2026 UNBS news says importers can create an account with a TIN and email, describes Customs integration and automatic ICC generation, and confirms destination inspection without PVoC, with a 15% CIF surcharge. It does not say every private postal recipient must independently register. Statutory regulation 8(1) affirmatively accepts a customs declaration upon arrival. An account interface does not displace that route without a universal registration duty. Do not claim a paper CN22 alone necessarily supplies every required customs data field.

Schedule 1 Part 3 item 1 excludes food from the low-value destination-inspection exemption, so tea remains inspectable and testable. Regulation 7(2) provides a 15% CIF surcharge and applicable inspection or other fees. Schedule 2 paragraph 2 sets a destination fee of 0.5% CIF (minimum USD 235, maximum USD 3,000), but expressly disapplies that fee below USD 1,300 CIF. Laboratory charges under paragraph 3, incidental storage and ordinary customs costs can remain. No exact fee total is promised.
